Rumours are afloat concerriitig the supposed terms of adjustment ol the Northeastern Boundary question which, we lather think þÿ indeed we may almost say we know þÿ are calculated to mislead the public nnnd. Our knowledge is indeed any thing but direct, and very far from being official. But two or three Missions and all their suites, seven Commissioners arid their clerks, are rather too many to keep a secret. Add to these two Heligations, more or less of whom are understood to have been consulted, and no one will wonder that the terms of the Boundary arrangement are supposed to be tolerably well understood here on the spot, though not correctly reported at a distance from the seat of Government. We will state them, therefore as we understand them. Lord Ashburton is believed to have held out long for the entire Madawaska settle, ment But the Maine Commissioners are said to have been as immovable as any lour pine slumps on the disputed territory. So Maine, under the arrangement, goes to the river St. John's, it is not unlikely, we learn, that the line which the Hutch arbiter decided for, the line of the St. John's and the St Francis, will be agreed to. But then Maine gets, what the Hutch King did not give her, the navigation ot the river; and this trebles the value ol ail her tall pine tress. and a large terntoiy heretofore supposed to belong to New York and Vermont, but winch turns out to lie north of the 45 th degree of latitude, and is therefore a part of Canada. It is said to be. and probably is, in consequence of this cession, that the United States Government agrees to pay a small sum to each ol the States of Maine and Massachusetts for the acres they have parted witn; not more than a quarter as much, however, us General Jackson offered to give t<> Maine alone, during his administration, in tiie year 1832 As to the various other questions, not connected with boundaries, which arc the subject of negotiation nothing is known. Every body is hard at work, however, and, judging from men's faces when met with u public, w e should say it is expected that every thing will come out about right. Though, as we have already intimidated, we speak without authority, we have no doubt of the general truth of what we have stated above. or enough fur ordinary ambition to have been instruiw.ntal and influential in the adjustment of differences which have been heretofore found so formidable and so repelling. We accordingly attended; and it is not easy to express our astonishment and gratification at what we saw. The various stages of cure, advanced in our presence, by the simple application, for about half a minute, or until a little warmth was felt by the patient, of the vapour of hydrocyanic acid, in a small phial, held up to the eye, with an aperture fitting the form of that organ ; the various nature of the diseases so assailed þÿ opacifies of the cornea, inflammation, cataract, amaurosis, iritis. þÿ&e Arc ; the various stages of relief which the patients had reached, with sometimes one eye opened to sight and pleasurable to look upon, and the other nearly blind and in its pristine deformity, to shew what had been achieved the various appearances of films removing, cataracts breaking up and being gradually re absorbed, pupils Sieing re developed and other altogether extraordinary symptoms of remedy and regeneration, filled us, we þÿrepeat with wonder and delight. SOMERVILLE, N. J., July 19th, 1842. This village is on the route from New York to þÿSchootey M s ountain, which is a cool and delightful retreat for the half melted and halfburned-up fashionables of that busy town, and during this remarkably hot weather hun dreds are floekinjr thither for a breath of air They come to this place by the rail road and go hence by stage coaches The following regulation tor running the cars indicates when the travellers arrive and depart. The ears will leave Somerville for New Yotk at 5 and 10$ A. M , and 3 P. M. þÿ Leave New- York þÿ B? steam-boat, pier No. IjBy N rail road, from foot North Hiver, of Liberty street, A 1 þÿo clock. AM. At 9 þÿo clock, A M. 2 þÿ P. IVt. I 2 þÿ P M. 4 þÿ P M. | 4j « P M. The cars will leave Elizabeth Port on the arrival of the boat and leave Elizabethtown on the arrival of the N. J. R. R. cars.

1 am told this village has hitherto been remarkable for not having a good tavern or house for travellers but in this respect there has beeu a great change of late. Mine host Sanderson, who keeps the Somerset! House is a new comer, and has fitted up the old rooms, built important additions and remodelled the establishment to such a degree that the old customers cannot readily recognize the house. Instead of being compelled to sleep upon feathers or sttaw in this hot weather, vou can have a line mattress and every thing which vour desire for comfort may indicate, þÿ' he bar-keeper is civil and strives to please to the utmost of his ability. I went to church on Sunday, and heard a goo 1 discourse, illustrating the importance of religious duties 1 have seldom seen a congregation of people whose appearance was more devout and Christian- like. Although the sparkling eyes of the dear ladies will shine let them he where they may, yet the fire was softened and made more bewitching to me by the influence of , the time and the occasion, as well as by what fell from the lips of the good man in the pulpit. On the day of the dale of my last letter, 1 visited the old stone house owned and occupied by the Hon. William Patterson, deceased, and formerly one of the judges of the Supreme Court of the United States. He was the Iriend of Aaron Burr, who. when a bov at Princeton College, made his borne here, for a part of his time, and after he graduated, pursued his studies in that antiquated mansion.

DA3T33L 'T'?' SSTTSTBi S92R &3«aTJ!!3T &3 AT'I3 It was there that the late Stephen Van Rensselaer of Albany found his accomplished lady. She was the daughter of Judge Patterson. Among the most amusing of my long rambles from this place, was one 1 made yesterday toward Princeton, in a neighbourhood once famous for rattle snakes. 1 stopped at the house of a farmer whose lady, although upwards of eighty years of age, is yet young in feeling, and is a fine specimen of the old school. She believes that those lattlesnakes possess the power to charm any thing, and to hold it in a trance till it is swallowed and destroyed. In support of what she so religiously believes, she related the following stories while I was partaking with hero! a delightful frugal repast. She knows that they are true for they were written down by one present when the events occuned.

give them to you m the words in which she has them recorded in the end of AJay, 1715, says her informant, stopping at an orchard by the road side to get some cherries, being three of us in company, we were enter taiued with the whole process ol a charm between a rattle snake and a hare, the hare being better than half grown. It happened thus ; one of the company in his search lor the best cherries espied the hare silting, and although he went close by her she did not move, till he (not suspecting the occasion ol her gentleness) gave tier a lash with his whip; this made her run about ten feet, and there sit down again. The gentleman not finding the cherries ripe immediately returned the same way, and near the place where he struck the hare, he spied a rattle-snake ; still not suspecting the charm, he went hack about twenty rods to a hedge to get a stick to kill the snake, and at his return found the snake reinoveu, and coiled in the same place from winch he had moved the hare. This put hun into immediate thoughts of looking for the hare again, and he soon spied her about ten feet ofl the snake, in the same place to which she had started when he struck her. ISlie was now lying down, but would sometimes raise herself on her fore feet, struggling as it were for life or to get away, but could never raise her hinder parts from the ground, and then would fall flat on her side again, panting vehemently. In this condition the hare and snake were when he called me; and though we all came

up within fifteen feet of the snake to have a full view of the whole, he took no notice at all of us, nor so much as gave a glance toward us. There we stood at least half an hour, the snake not alteiing a jut, hut the hare often struggling and falling on its side again till at last the hare lay still as dead for some time Then the snake moved out of his coil, and slid gently and smoothly on toward the hare, his colors at that time being ten times more glorious and shining than at other times As the snake moved along, the hate happened to fetch another struggle, upon which the snake made a stop, lying at his length, till the hare had lain quiet again, for a short space; and then he advanced again till he came up to the hinder parts ol the hare, which, in all this operation hud been toward the snake. Then he made a survey all ovei the hare, raising part of his body above it, then turned off and went to the bead and nose of the hare, after that to the ears, took the ears in his mouth one alter the other, working each apatt in his month as a man does a

wafer to moisten it, then returned to the nose again and took the face into his mouth, straining and gathering his lips sometimes by one side of his mouth sometimes by the other ; at the shoulders he was a long time puzzled, halting and stretching the hare out at length, and straining forward, first one side of his mouth, then the other, till he got at last the whole body into his throat. Then we went to him, and taking the twist band ofl from my fiat, I made a noose and put it about his neck. This made him at length very furious, but we having secured him, put him into one end af a wallet, and carried him on horseback five miles to Mr. J B þÿ s house where we lodged that night, with a design to have him sent to lJr. C at Williamsburg; but Mr. B was so careful ot bis slaves, that he would not let him be put into his boat for fear he should get loose and mischief them ; therefore the next morning we killed him, and took the hare out of his belly: the head of the hare had begun to be digested, and the hair falling off, having lain about eighteen hours in the snake's belly. Another story was as follows ! þÿ In my youth, says the informant, I was bear-hunting in the woods, and having straggled from my companions. 1 was entertained on mv return with the relation of a pleasant encounter, between a dog and a rattlesnake about a squirrel. The snake had got the head and shoulders of the squirrel into his mouth, which being something too large for his throat, it took him some time to moisten

the for of the squirrel to make it slip down þÿ The dog took this advantage, seized the hinder parts of the squirrel and tugged with all his might The snake on the other side would not let go his hold for a long time, fearing he might be bruised by the þÿdog r s unning away with him, he gave up his prey to the dog ; the dog ate the squirrel and felt no harm. I intended to write you another letter from this place, and indeed to remain here a week or two longer, but a friend of none, a chum of former days, has invited me to go with him to Washington and upon the spur of the moment 1 have consented We shall leave to-morrow morning, taking the cars hence to Elizabethtown or the stage to New Brunswick this evening, where we shall take the cars to Philadelphia I have never been at the seat of government having been cautioned by those who love me most to keep away from politicians and aloof from their schemes and machinations But in this instance hot as the weather is, and fascinating as mv present pursuits are, I have concluded to lake a look at what is doing in Washington I hope I shall see what will compensate me for the journey. Yours truly, JO SYKES.

GENERAL ORDERS. General Lord Hill finds it necessary to resign the command of the army on account of his lordship's present state of health, and her Majesty has been graciously pleased to accept iiis lordship's resignation. When Lord Hill assumed the command which he now resigns, he expressed, in gene ral orders, his confident hope, that trom the general and other officers, as well as Irom the public departments ot the army, he would receive that support which should enable him to fulfil the important trust reposed in him. That hope has not been disappointed, but, on the contrary, realised beyond Lord Hill's most sanguine expectation. The conduct of the troops has, both in the field and in quarters, furnished, during Lord Hill's command of them an example of discipline, regularity, and general efficiency not to be surpassed; and the officers have by their devotion to their duty enabled his lordship to maintain the army in tuat cieditable state. The officers have, therefore, established their claim to Lord llill's lasting gratitude and esteem. His lordship cannot, then, bin with painful feelings take leave ol officers, non commissioned ofliceis and soldiers, whose conduct has been so uniformly approved by their Sovereign and by their country. These feelings are, ho wevei . greatlv aiie viated and consoled by the reflection, that the command of the army is now 10 be resumed by the Duke of Wellington, the ever vigilant and most influential guardian of its interests, and whose achievements have raised its cha-
racter to the highest pinnacle ot giory. þÿ By command of the Right Hou. General Lord Hill, Commanding in Ciue.t. Horse Guards Aug. 15 John Macijonald. Adj. Gen.

The -new plan for the West India Mail Packet service, which lias been ottered by the Steam Navigation Company to the Government, and which it is understood lias been agreed upon and will come into operation on the 1st ol October, has lately been primed. According to this plan, a steamer engaged on that part of the service which is called the " Out Atlantic." is to leave Southampton, on the 1st and 15th of each month (perhaps a day later,) and will, while Falmouth is retained as a port, call there for the outward mails, leaving on the 15th and 17th. She will then proceed to Corunna, remaining 12 hours for coals, and thence to Fnnchal, Madeira' where she will remain to land her mails for a period not exceeding 6 hours. She then goes on to St. Thomas's, and there deliveis her outward mails to 1 steamers, waiting for her, and the destination of which will presently be explained. Having thus dispersed her mails, she in tier turn becomes one of the 4 vessels to await the arrival of the next steam, er. that wiil follow from Europe in 15 davs. The voyage from Falmouth to St. Thomas's is estimated at about 19 days and a half. The first of the 4 steamers receiving her mails at St. Thomas's sets out on the Demerara route, it being calculated tlwi she is to start about 22 days after the fi st steamer left England. "r tvvo davs and a half after Hie arrival of that vessel at St Thomas's On her route she delivers mails at the tollowing places, in the order in which they are here set down : þÿ Tortolo, St Kitt's, Nevis,

Montserral, Antigua, Goadaloupe. Dominieai Martinique. St. I.ncia. Barbadoes and Demerara, calling at all the same islands in the reverse order on her way back to .St. Tho. mis'#, where she returns after an estimated absence of 14 days 5 hours. For stoppage at each island, both on the route to Detnerara and back, two hours at most are allowed, and at Demerara she will remain to coal until 30 days 15 hours reckoned from the time when the outward mail left Falmouth At Barbadoes, where she will arrive in 25 days 8 hours, reckoned from the same distance, she will find a small steamer destined for the Trinidad station, which will necessarily visit St Vincents. Grenada, Tobago, and Trinidad, touching at the same places on her way back to Barbadoes, and occupying by hei total route from and to Barbadoes, 6 days 13 hours. The stav at Trinidad is so to be regulated that she may leave it in 29 dnvs 6 hours Irom the date of the departure of the outwards mails from Falmouth, and when she has returned to Barbadoes, she is to wait there fir the next arrival from St. Thomas's when she will repeal her voyage as before. The second ol the four stenmeis which receives at St, Thomas's the mails from Europe. and which, like the first, starts in 22 days from thedepaiture from Falmouth, is destined for the Jamaica station, and visits in succession San Juan (Porto Kico.) Gape Haytien. St. Jago de Cuba, and Jamaica, and ref Virus to St. Thomas's in 14 riavs 2 hours, having touched at the same places on h'-r

journey hack. This steamer will not, however, take the Jamaica out mails, hut irerelv call for the correspondence from thn' The Jamaica out mails will he taken e I third stevtner from St. Thomas's, ties, moil for the ilav'tinnah station, win ,i w-b pro-

The fourth of the steamers at St Thomas's is destined for the Bermuda station, performing her journey there and hack in 12 days 20 hours, and is employed in receiving the home mail's collected by other steamers, and the outward mails for Bermuda, it thev arrive at St. '1 homas's before midnight on the 22d day after the outward mails leave Falmouth For the transmission of mails to Mexico a steamer is stationed at Hnvannah, where the mails will arrive in 20 j days after they have left England, and will proceed fiist to Vera Gruz. and then to Tampico. returning to Ha varinah in 20 days. Curious Ciock þÿ M. Schwilgue says the Courier tin Ihts Kit in is putting the finishing hand to ihe repairs of the astronomical clock of the cathedral of Strasbourg, after having

devoted four years to the work. It will he ready about the end of the month, and us inauguration will take place at the fetes given in honor of the Scientific Congress In this curious piece mechanism the revolutions of of the sun, the moon, and the planets, are marked down with scientific exactness Seven figur represent the seven davs of the week, s each appearing in its turn on the day allotted to it The four ages come forward to strike the quarters, and the hideous skeleton Death strikes the hours. At noon the Twelve Apostles advance in succession to bend down before the ligure of our Saviour, who gives them the benediction. At the same moment a cock claps his wirigs and crows three times, through the vaulted roof of the cathedral. All the persons who have seen this work the Courier du Bas Khin adds agree in consid ering it one of the most curious pieces of clockwork in Europe.

We have elsewhere reported what the French newspapers say upon the subject 'The animadversionsof the British pressare so strongly indicative of angry political feeling thai we think it but prudent not to report them.
